newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajiks undertake risky rebel-for-hostage swap.
newsitem.headline: Tajiks undertake risky rebel-for-hostage swap.

text.p: The Tajik government hoped to complete a risky rebels-for-hostages swap early on Saturday, but it was unclear whether the Islamic group holding 14 foreign and Russian hostages would keep their end of the deal.

The complicated swap proceedure was started late on Friday when rebel leader Bakhram Sadirov allowed three hostages to leave the captors' base on a mountain top in a barren rocky region about 80 km (50 miles) from the capital Dushanbe.

"We are ready. Get these people over to us and we will release our people (the hostages)," Sadirov told a Russian diplomat who was negotiating by walkie talkie a few kilometres (miles) away. The conversation was recorded by Russian television.

The three hostages were expected to return up the mountain with the diplomat, Gennady Sizov, and a group of rebels flown in by Tajik authorities for the exchange. Itar-Tass news agency reported they had set out on the difficult journey on dirt roads early on Saturday local time.

After the arriving rebels -- who were shown on Russian television earlier in the day with their hands tied behind their backs under Tajik government control -- had been united with their comrades, all 14 hostages were due to be freed.
Russian and Tajik officials negotiated with Sadirov throughout the day and night, and described a tense situation.
"He (Sadirov) is in a very agitated state," Russian Deputy Prime Minister Vitaly Ignatenko told Russian television. "His demands are becoming more severe...but we have met them all."
Russia, whose soldiers help police the border with Afghanistan, has appealed for the early release of the captives.

The swap deal agreed to by the Tajik government apparently leaves open the risk that Sadirov could keep the hostages as well as the Russian diplomat overseeing the exchange after the additional rebels arrived.

"I'm afraid if we send them (Sizov and the returning three hostages) all up there, they will take them as hostages and set new conditions," G. Mirzoyev, a leader of the Tajik presidential guard at the scene, told Russian television.
The hostages include three U.N. observers -- two from Switzerland and one from Ukraine -- four Russian journalists and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency.

Tajikistan's security minister was also seized last weekend when he tried to negotiate with the hostage-takers, who once backed the former Soviet republic's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.
Questions remained on Saturday about the fate of one of the U.N. observers. Sadirov said on Thursday he had killed an observer, but on Friday he told Ignatenko that the report was untrue.
The hostage crisis has highlighted the instability of Tajikistan, an impoverished former Soviet republic bordering Afghanistan and China.
Armed groups opposed to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov are scattered across the country and some fighters, such as those loyal to Sadirov and his brother Rivzon, are based in Afghanistan.
